item.title: Understand the System Before Changing It
item.description:
One thing I’ve learned over the years is that good architecture often starts with understanding the system you already have.

Before changing something, I usually invest some time looking at how requests actually flow, where the dependencies are, what the failure points might be, and perhaps most importantly… why things ended up the way they are.

Sometimes there’s a very good reason. Sometimes the reason is simply that the system evolved over time. Either way, understanding the context usually leads to better decisions than jumping straight to a solution.

item.title: What programming was like in 1985
item.description:
Jonh Graham-Cumming, a programmer from 1985, shows what programming was like back then, according to him it was quite common to write code on sheets of paper because of the limitations of the machines they used in those days.

Today, when we see programmers at companies like Facebook writing code on modern machines, we don’t imagine how difficult it was to get here.

However, the technology industry has evolved extraordinarily and quickly in recent decades. The image below shows the result of configuring a machine that put packaging on bottles, the algorithm was developed by Jonh.

item.title: Case Sensitive
item.description:
“Case sensitive” is a term indicating that text is sensitive to letter case, meaning it distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters.

We’ll see how it works in practice by looking at the situations below:

Case Sensitive

texto is different from Texto, because the second word starts with a capitalized consonant.

Case Insensitive

texto is the same as Texto, there is no distinction between letter cases.

A related concept joins words and capitalizes the letters at the beginning of each word, called CamelCase.

item.title: The CamelCase Convention
item.description:
CamelCase (camel case) is the practice of writing compound words or phrases with their elements joined, without spaces, and the first letter of each element capitalized, meaning the uppercase letters “jump” out among the lowercase ones like a camel’s humps.

Example: “meuComputador, “jogoDeFutebol” or “linguagemProgramacao”.
